t:
(a) 
For fiscal year 1996 the Secretary of Transportation shall distribute the obligation limitation for Federal-aid highways by allocation in the ratio which sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to each State for such fiscal year bear to the total of the sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to all the States for such fiscal year.
 
    (b) 
During the period October 1 through December 31, 1995, no State shall obligate more than 25 per centum of the amount distributed to such State under subsection (a), and the total of all State obligations during such period shall not exceed 12 per centum of the total amount distributed to all States under such subsection.
 
    (c) 
Notwithstanding subsections (a) and (b), the Secretary shall—

        (1) 
provide all States with authority sufficient to prevent lapses of sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that have been apportioned to a State;
 
        (2) 
after August 1, 1996, revise a distribution of the funds made available under subsection (a) if a State will not obligate the amount distributed during that fiscal year and redistribute sufficient amounts to those States able to obligate amounts in addition to those previously distributed during that fiscal year giving priority to those States having large unobligated balances of funds apportioned under sections 103(e)(4), 104, and 144 of title 23, United States Code, and under sections 1013(c) and 1015 of Public Law 102–240; and
 
        (3) 
not distribute amounts authorized for administrative expenses and funded from the administrative takedown authorized by section 104(a), title 23 U.S.C, the Federal lands highway program, the intelligent transportation systems program, and amounts made available under sections 1040, 1047, 1064, 6001, 6005, 6006, 6023, and 6024 of Public Law 102–240, and 49 U.S.C. 5316, 5317, and 5338: Provided, That amounts made available under section 6005 of Public Law 102–240 shall be subject to the obligation limitation for Federal-aid highways and highway safety construction programs under the head “Federal-Aid Highways” in this Act.
  
    (d) 
During the period October 1 through December 31, 1995, the aggregate amount of obligations under section 157 of title 23, United States Code, for projects covered under section 147 of the Surface Transportation Assistance Act of 1978, section 9 of the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1981, sections 131(b), 131(j), and 404 of Public Law 97–424, sections 1061, 1103 through 1108, 4008, and 6023(b)(8) and 6023(b)(10) of Public Law 102–240, and for projects authorized by Public Law 99–500 and Public Law 100–17, shall not exceed $277,431,840.
 
    (e) 
During the period August 2 through September 30, 1996, the aggregate amount which may be obligated by all States shall not exceed 2.5 percent of the aggregate amount of funds apportioned or allocated to all States—

        (1) 
under sections 104 and 144 of title 23, United States Code, and 1013(c) and 1015 of Public Law 102–240, and
 
        (2) 
for highway assistance projects under section 103(e)(4) of title 23, United States Code,
   which would not be obligated in fiscal year 1996 if the total amount of the obligation limitation provided for such fiscal year in this Act were utilized.

    (f) 
Paragraph (e) shall not apply to any State which on or after August 1, 1996, has the amount distributed to such State under paragraph (a) for fiscal year 1996 reduced under paragraph (c)(2).

fable.w: The tempting reading is that because States are named throughout, they are outside parties taking part in a federal decision. But the section only sets a formula for distributing and redistributing highway obligation authority and caps on State obligations; States are funding recipients, not consulted parties. There is no comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, consultation requirement, or right to sue.
fable.s: the Secretary of Transportation shall distribute the obligation limitation for Federal-aid highways by allocation

qwen_block.w: This section establishes a formula for the Secretary of Transportation to distribute federal funds to states. It does not require the Secretary to consult with states, the public, or any outside entities before making the distribution decision; the allocation is determined mechanically by statutory ratios. While states are involved as recipients, the process described is an administrative distribution of funds, not a participatory decision-making process involving outside input.
qwen_block.s: For fiscal year 1996 the Secretary of Transportation shall distribute the obligation limitation for Federal-aid highways by allocation in the ratio which sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to each State for such fiscal year bear to the total of the sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to all the States for such fiscal year.

opus.w: This section sets formulas and caps for how the Secretary of Transportation distributes and redistributes highway obligation limits among States. The States only receive funds and must follow spending limits; the Secretary is not required to consult or coordinate with them before deciding. It reads like a closer call because States appear throughout, but receiving funds is excluded in the same way grants and benefits are. There is also no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking authority or right to sue.
opus.s: after August 1, 1996, revise a distribution of the funds made available under subsection (a) if a State will not obligate the amount distributed during that fiscal year and redistribute sufficient amounts to those States able to obligate amounts in addition to those previously distributed during that fiscal year
opus.b:
1. **Reasoning:** The tempting reading is that States take part because the section is all about distributions to States and State obligations, and it says the Secretary will redistribute funds "if a State will not obligate the amount distributed." That reading fails the definition. The States here only receive federal-aid highway money and are bound by spending limits. Nothing requires or allows the Secretary to consult, coordinate with or hear from States or anyone else before deciding. The section also has no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking authority or right to sue. Funding distributions are like grants and benefits, which the definition excludes.

2. **Label:**

qwen_chat.w: This section describes the mechanical distribution of federal funds to states based on statutory formulas. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or input from outside parties (like states, tribes, or the public) in the decision-making process. The interaction is administrative and mandatory, not participatory in the sense of seeking advice or coordinating policy with external entities. The definition excludes applications for grants/benefits, and this is essentially the allocation of such benefits.
qwen_chat.s: For fiscal year 1996 the Secretary of Transportation shall distribute the obligation limitation for Federal-aid highways by allocation in the ratio which sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to each State for such fiscal year bear to the total of the sums authorized to be appropriated for Federal-aid highways that are apportioned or allocated to all the States for such fiscal year.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the Secretary interacts with States (which are outside the federal government) to distribute funds and revise distributions, this constitutes participation. However, the definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants" and general administrative coordination. The interaction here is purely mechanical and statutory (distributing funds based on formulas), not a consultation or coordination process where outside parties influence a discretionary decision through advice, comment, or negotiation. The States are recipients of funds, not participants in the decision-making process in the sense defined (e.g., advisory boards, public hearings, consultation on policy).
